courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: Magnetic flux Φ_B = ∫B·dA = B*A*cos θ, measured in webers (Wb = T·m² = V·s), where θ is the angle between B and the OUTWARD NORMAL to the loop's plane — flux is maximum (BA) when the loop's plane is perpendicular to B and zero when the field lies in the plane of the loop.

Faraday's law of induction, ε = −N dΦ_B/dt in volts: the emf induced in a closed loop equals the negative of the time rate of change of the flux linking it, valid whether the change is caused by a changing B, by a changing enclosed area, by a changing orientation, or by any combination; the average emf over a stated interval is N|ΔΦ_B|/Δt, which is not the peak or instantaneous value.

Faraday's own conclusion that the mere existence of magnetic flux is not sufficient to induce an emf — the flux must be CHANGING — so a stationary magnet inside a loop, or a loop moving entirely within a uniform field, produces no current however large the flux.

Lenz's law as the physical content of the minus sign: the induced current flows in the sense whose magnetic field opposes the CHANGE in flux through the enclosed area, giving the deck's three rules (induced field opposite to B when the external flux is increasing, along B when it is decreasing, zero when the flux is constant), with the sense of the current then read off by the right-hand grip rule and only the field within the loop counted.

Motional emf |ε| = B*L*v for a rod of length L sliding at speed v on rails with B perpendicular to the circuit plane, giving I = BLv/R and a retarding force F = B*I*L = B²L²v/R that always opposes the motion, so that the mechanical power Fv = B²L²v²/R exactly equals the I²R dissipated — the energy-conservation argument behind Lenz's law.

The a.c. generator: an N-turn coil of area A rotating at angular speed ω = 2πf in a uniform field gives Φ_B = BA cos(ωt) and ε = N*B*A*ω*sin(ωt), with ε_peak = NBAω, ε_rms = ε_peak/√2 and a full-cycle average of exactly zero; the emf is zero when the flux is maximum and maximum when the flux is zero.

Charge circulated by a flux change, q = ∫I dt = N|ΔΦ_B|/R coulombs, which depends only on the total flux change and the circuit resistance and NOT on how quickly the change occurs — a faster change simply gives a larger current for a proportionately shorter time.

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: Applications of the definite integral to volumes: a region in the plane revolved about a fixed line (the axis of revolution) generates a solid of revolution whose volume is obtained by slicing it into thin pieces and integrating the cross-sectional area, V = ∫ₐᵇ A(s) ds.

The deck's four-step setup procedure: sketch the region and identify the axis of revolution (which fixes the variable of integration), sketch the cross-section as a disc, washer or shell and choose the matching formula, determine the boundaries of the solid, then set up and evaluate the definite integral.

The disc method, V = π∫ₐᵇ[f(x)]²dx about a horizontal axis (and π∫[g(y)]²dy about a vertical one), valid only when the region is flush against the axis so every cross-section is a full circle with no cavity.

The washer method, V = π∫ₐᵇ([R]² − [r]²)ds, with R the distance from the axis to the boundary farthest from it and r the distance to the nearest boundary, used whenever the region is offset from the axis; the standing trap of writing π∫(R − r)² instead of π∫(R² − r²) is treated explicitly.

The shell method, V = 2π∫ₐᵇ(radius)(height)ds, derived from unrolling a thin cylindrical shell into a rectangle of length 2π·radius, with the radius entering to the first power only; shells integrate in the variable opposite to the one used by discs and washers for the same axis.

Rotation about lines other than the coordinate axes — y = k and x = h — where every radius must be rewritten as a distance (f(x) − k, |x − h|) before squaring, and where the outer radius may belong to the lower curve when the axis lies above the region.

Practical setup skills: locating the limits by solving the bounding curves simultaneously, choosing between integrating in x and in y (including inverting y = f(x) to x = g(y)), splitting a region when the bounding curve changes partway, cross-checking a shell answer against a washer answer, and recognising a negative result as a swapped pair of radii.

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: Modularisation is defined as the process of dividing a program's functionality into independent modules such that each independent module has everything it needs to implement only a part of the program's functionality, and decomposition is shown to be embedded in that definition, since separating an application's code into different modules and functions is itself the act of decomposing it.

The motivation is developed from the five-thousand-line function that cannot be changed safely because a change to one part affects other parts, and is set against the deck's five stated advantages of modularisation (parallel work by several people, easier management and extension, easier understanding of small units, reuse within the program or in another program, and faster design, development, testing and publishing) and its five stated disadvantages (longer execution time, increased storage size, longer compilation and loading time, increased inter-module communication problems, and more initial design time).

Module independence is presented through the single responsibility principle, which demands that a module have no more than one responsibility and not depend on other modules, and is measured by two quantities the students must be able to state exactly: cohesion, the extent to which the functions in a module work together to achieve the ultimate aim of the module, which should be high, and coupling, the extent to which modules depend on other modules before performing their function, which should be low; a car's steering wheel, radiator, battery and brake serve as the worked analogy.

Information hiding requires that the data structures and processing details of one module not be accessible to other modules and that modules pass only that much information as is required to accomplish the software functions, with three benefits: communication through controlled interfaces, a decreased probability of adverse effects, and restriction of the effects of a change in one component on other components.

Refactoring is defined as modifying a software system to improve the internal structure of the design without changing its external behaviour, checking the existing design for flaws such as redundancy and poorly constructed algorithms and data structures, and is illustrated by splitting a component that performs four weakly related functions into four components each exhibiting high cohesion, which yields easier integration, testing and maintenance.

Structural partitioning applies to hierarchical architectural styles and comes in two forms: horizontal, in which control modules communicate between functions and execute them at the cost of passing more data across module interfaces and a more complex control flow, and vertical, in which top-level control modules perform decision-making and little processing while low-level worker modules perform all input, computation and output; its benefits are easier testing and maintenance, slowly spreading negative impacts, and easy extension.

The second deck defines software architecture as the structure of the system containing the components of a program or system, the attributes or properties of those components and the relationships between them, explains why architecture matters for stakeholder communication, early design decisions and intellectual models of the system, and then distinguishes the three levels of software pattern (high-level architectural patterns often considered equivalent to software architecture, medium-level design patterns often considered equivalent to software components, and low-level language-specific idioms termed coding patterns) before contrasting the two generic design approaches, top-down for systems designed from scratch with unknown details and bottom-up for systems built from an existing system's primitives with abstraction increasing at each higher level, neither of which is individually practicable.

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Determination of the magnetic permeability of free space μ₀ from the axial magnetic field of a single-turn circular loop, using the working formula B(z) = μ₀ I R² / [2 (R² + z²)^(3/2)], where B(z) is the flux density in tesla at axial distance z (m) from the centre, I is the loop current in amperes, R is the loop radius in metres, and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A ≡ 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m; at z = 0 this reduces to the maximum value B(0) = μ₀I/2R.

Apparatus: a circular loop of radius R, a DC power supply, an ammeter, a movable magnetic (Hall) probe and a tesla meter; the virtual rig defaults to Coil 1 with R = 0.10 m and a current set to I = 1 A.

Procedure: place the probe at the centre of the coil (z = 0) and record B on the tesla meter, then increase z in steps of 2 cm (2, 4, 6 … up to 38 cm) recording B each time for 20 readings in all, and repeat the whole set for Coil 2, Coil 3 etc. of different radius — the 20 readings supply the spread of points needed for a straight-line fit and average out reading scatter, while the different coils test that μ₀ is independent of R and I.

Data analysis: for every reading compute the factor x = I R² / [2 (R² + z²)^(3/2)] in A/m, plot B (y-axis, in tesla) against that factor (x-axis, in A/m) to obtain the straight line B = μ₀x through the origin in the form y = mx, and take the gradient m = ΔB/Δx, which equals μ₀ directly in T·m/A = H/m; if the factor is computed without I the gradient equals μ₀I instead and μ₀ = gradient / I.

Unit handling and errors: the downloaded Excel sheet lists z in cm and B in nT while R is in metres, so z must be divided by 100 and B multiplied by 10⁻⁹ before plotting or the gradient is out by about 10⁹; systematic errors come from probe misalignment off the axis, a mislocated z = 0 origin, tesla-meter zero error, stray fields (Earth's field, nearby magnets or steel) and ammeter calibration, while random reading scatter is reduced by using the line of best fit over all 20 points.

Deck faults to flag: the B(z) equation and the analysis 'factor' appear only as dropped images, the slide heading is truncated at 'Magnetic-Permeability-of-', the sample data table skips from z = 10 cm to z = 26 cm, μ₀ is quoted as T·m/A in the theory slide but H/m in the summary (equivalent units, not a contradiction), and the summary sheet misprints 'REPUTATION between like poles' for REPULSION.

courses.name: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
weekTopics: The "Makers of Nigeria" deck profiles nine Nigerians from politics, activism, literature, music, law and sport, opening with Herbert Macaulay (1864-1946), tagged the father of Nigerian nationalism, who protested colonial water rates, land issues and railway finance management in the 1920s and founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party in 1923 as Nigeria's first political party, whose members were the first to sit in the legislative council and which merged with the Nigerian Youth Movement in the late 1930s to form the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons.

Obafemi Awolowo (1909-1987) is presented as first premier of the western region from 1954 to 1960, Nigeria's foremost federalist and leader of the Action Group whose campaign for a federal constitution was realised in the 1954 Lyleton Constitution, and as leader of the opposition against the Balewa-led government under the Northern People's Party, while Nnamdi Azikiwe (1904-1996) is given as the last governor-general from 1960 to 1963, the first elected president from 1963 to 1966 in the first republic, a co-founder of the NCNC who joined politics in 1944 and the inspiration for the radical multi-ethnic Zikist movement.

Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (1900-1978), the "Lioness of Lisabi", mobilised market women and organised the 1953 Abeokuta conference that produced the Federation of Nigerian Women's Societies, and died on 13 April 1978 from injuries sustained when, aged 76, she was thrown from a second-story window during the 18 February 1977 military raid on the Lagos residence of her son Fela Anikulapo-Kuti (1938-1997), credited as the creator of Afrobeat in the early 1970s.

Chinua Achebe (1930-2013) is covered for Things Fall Apart (1958), the most widely read book in modern African literature, for heading the Biafra Broadcasting Service, and for becoming deputy national vice president of the People's Redemption Party in 1983 and writing The Trouble with Nigeria; Wole Soyinka (1934-Present) for his 22-month imprisonment in 1967 as a 33-year-old graduate, his flight from treason charges in 1994, and the 1986 Nobel Prize for Literature as the first African, dedicated to the imprisoned Nelson Mandela.

The deck closes with Gani (Ganiyu Oyesola) Fawehinmi (1938-2009), who began practising in Lagos in 1965, became known as "the people's lawyer" through pro bono work, campaigned on human rights for 40 years and pressed to re-open the case of Dele Giwa, killed by a parcel bomb in 1986, before dying of cancer in 2009; and Nwankwo Kanu (1976-Present), whose contribution won Nigeria the 1996 Olympic Gold medal past Brazil and Argentina, who won the African Footballer award, the Premier League, the UEFA Champions League and the UEFA Cup, and who serves as a UNICEF ambassador.

The Week 11 Summary PDF pairs the Makers of Nigeria with a Nigerian diaspora strand covering remittances as a key source of foreign exchange and major contributor to GDP, the diaspora's roots in pre-modern migrations, the slave trade and contemporary economic migration, the educational and professional achievements of Nigerians in the United States, the concept of "Japa", and the need for strategies to harness diaspora potential while addressing criminal activity by a minority; the closing slide also names Burna Boy, Wizkid, Davido and Rema.

courses.name: Introduction to Web Technologies
weekTopics: Web application security terminology separating a vulnerability (a weakness in design, implementation or configuration) from a threat (potential harm), with security defined as protecting the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data.

The five named vulnerabilities — SQL Injection (malicious SQL in user input manipulating the database, e.g. 'OR 1=1--'), Cross-Site Scripting (scripts injected into pages other users view, causing data theft or session hijacking), Cross-Site Request Forgery (tricking an already-authenticated user into an unwanted action), other Injection Attacks (Command Injection, XML Injection), and Security Misconfiguration (e.g. plaintext database credentials in config files).

Seven best practices matched to the vulnerabilities they answer: Input Validation with parameterised queries against SQLi, Output Encoding with Content Security Policy against XSS, Authentication and Authorization with 2FA and role/permission-based privileges, Session Management with unique tokens and expiry against CSRF, Security Headers (HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options), Regular Updates and Security Testing (vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, code reviews); plus the Web Application Firewall as an additional layer filtering and monitoring HTTP/HTTPS requests, and secure development via Secure Coding, Code Review and DevSecOps.

Server deployment and hosting: server, deployment and hosting defined separately; physical versus virtual servers; server operating systems (Ubuntu, CentOS, Windows Server) and server roles (Apache/Nginx, MySQL/PostgreSQL, Microsoft Exchange); and the four hosting options — on-premises (complete control, heavy maintenance), cloud on AWS/Azure/GCP (scalability, flexibility, cost-efficiency, e.g. AWS Elastic Beanstalk), VPS (a partitioned physical server balancing control and cost, e.g. DigitalOcean) and shared hosting (cheapest, limited performance, e.g. Bluehost).

Scalability and performance optimisation: horizontal scaling (adding machines/instances, achieved by load balancing) versus vertical scaling (upgrading CPU, memory or storage on the existing server), load balancing with NGINX or AWS Elastic Load Balancing to remove bottlenecks and add fault tolerance, caching in a temporary layer, CDNs such as Cloudflare delivering content from servers closer to users, database optimisation through indexing, and front-end optimisation through minification, responsive images and lazy loading.

Monitoring, debugging, testing and continuous integration: monitoring through metrics, alerts and logging (New Relic, Datadog), debugging through error handling, debugging tools such as Chrome DevTools and version control with Git, load testing with Apache JMeter and Gatling, unit/integration/end-to-end testing, and CI pipelines with Jenkins or Travis CI that build, test and deploy on each commit; plus server security and maintenance measures — firewalls, patching, intrusion detection systems, strong authentication, backups and a disaster recovery plan.

questions.q: The region under y = 3x, above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 2 is revolved about the x-axis. Use the disc method to find the volume.
questions.concept: Disc method about the x-axis
questions.why:
The axis is the x-axis, so the radius of each disc is the y-value: R(x) = 3x. V = π∫₀²(3x)²dx = π∫₀²9x²dx = π[3x³]₀² = 24π cubic units.

6π forgets to square the radius, π∫₀²3x dx; 24 drops the π; 48π uses the shell coefficient 2π in a disc formula.

questions.q: A rectangle with corners (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 2) and (0, 2) is revolved about the x-axis. Use the disc formula V = π∫ₐᵇ[R(x)]²dx to find the volume of the solid.
questions.concept: Disc with a constant radius
questions.why:
Every point of the top edge y = 2 is at distance 2 from the axis, so R(x) = 2 is constant and the solid is a cylinder. V = π∫₀³2²dx = π∫₀³4dx = π[4x]₀³ = 12π cubic units, which agrees with πr²h = π(2)²(3).

6π forgets to square the radius; 18π squares the length 3 instead of the radius 2 (π∫₀²9dy); 24π doubles the π.

questions.q: The region bounded by x = 2y, the y-axis and the line y = 3 is revolved about the y-axis. Find the volume.
questions.concept: Disc method in y about the y-axis
questions.why:
The axis is the y-axis, so integrate in y with the radius R(y) = 2y running from y = 0 to y = 3. V = π∫₀³(2y)²dy = π∫₀³4y²dy = π[4y³/3]₀³ = 36π cubic units (a cone of radius 6 and height 3).

9π forgets to square the radius; 72π uses 2π; 18π squares the 2 but not the y, giving π∫₀³4y dy.

questions.q: The region between y = x³ and y = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 is revolved about the x-axis. Which is the outer radius R(x) in the washer formula?
questions.concept: Identifying the outer radius of a washer
questions.why:
R is the boundary farther from the axis of revolution. On [0, 1], x ≥ x³ (test x = 1/2: 1/2 > 1/8), and distance from the x-axis is the y-value, so the line y = x is the outer boundary: R(x) = x, and r(x) = x³.

x³ is the inner radius; 1 is the right-hand limit of integration, not a radius; x − x³ is the height of a strip, which belongs to the shell integrand, not to a washer.

questions.q: The region between y = x + 1 and y = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume.
questions.concept: Washer method about the x-axis
questions.why:
The region does not touch the axis, so it is a washer with R(x) = x + 1 (the farther boundary) and r(x) = 1. V = π∫₀²[(x + 1)² − 1²]dx = π∫₀²(x² + 2x)dx = π[x³/3 + x²]₀² = π(8/3 + 4) = 20π/3 cubic units.

8π/3 integrates (R − r)² = x², the difference squared instead of the squares subtracted; 2π forgets to square either radius; 26π/3 adds the squares instead of subtracting them.

questions.q: The region under y = 4 − x, above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 4 is revolved about the y-axis. Use the shell method to find the volume.
questions.concept: Shell method about the y-axis
questions.why:
For a shell the radius is x (distance from the y-axis) and the height is f(x) = 4 − x. V = 2π∫₀⁴x(4 − x)dx = 2π∫₀⁴(4x − x²)dx = 2π[2x² − x³/3]₀⁴ = 2π(32 − 64/3) = 2π(32/3) = 64π/3 cubic units.

128π/3 squares the height, 2π∫x(4 − x)²dx; 32π/3 uses π instead of 2π; 16π leaves out the radius x and integrates 2π∫(4 − x)dx.

questions.q: The region under y = x, above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 1 is revolved about the line y = −2. What are the outer and inner radii?
questions.concept: Radii measured from a shifted axis
questions.why:
Every radius is a distance from the line y = −2. The far boundary y = x is at distance x − (−2) = x + 2, so R = x + 2; the near boundary y = 0 is at distance 0 − (−2) = 2, so r = 2. The region does not reach the axis, so there is a hole and the inner radius is not zero.

R = x, r = 0 ignores the shift entirely; R = x − 2 shifts in the wrong direction; R = x + 2, r = 0 shifts the outer radius but fills in a hole that is really there.

questions.q: A region is revolved about the y-axis and the disc or washer method is to be used. In which variable is the integral taken, and how must the boundary curves be written?
options: dx, with the curves written as y = f(x)
dy, with the curves written as x = f(y)
dy, with the curves written as y = f(x)
dx, with the curves written as x = f(y)
questions.concept: The axis of revolution fixes the variable of integration
questions.why:
For discs and washers the slices are perpendicular to the axis of revolution and the integral runs along it. Revolving about the y-axis means the discs are stacked in y, so the integral is dy and each radius must be a distance measured horizontally, which needs the curves in the form x = f(y). For example x = y² + 1 or x = 3.

dx with y = f(x) is the set-up for the x-axis; the other two mix a variable of integration with curves written in the wrong form, so the radius would not be a function of the integration variable.

questions.q: The region under y = √x, above the x-axis, from x = 1 to x = 3 is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume. Show your working.
questions.concept: Disc method with a square-root radius
questions.why:
The axis is the x-axis, so R(x) = √x with a = 1, b = 3. Squaring removes the root: [√x]² = x. V = π∫₁³(√x)²dx = π∫₁³x dx = π[x²/2]₁³ = π(9/2 − 1/2) = 4π.

Final answer: 4π cubic units (also accepted: 12.57). The working must show the radius squared to x and the bracket evaluated at both limits. Integrating √x without squaring gives (2/3)(3√3 − 1)π and is wrong; π(9/2) = 9π/2 forgets the lower limit.

questions.q: The region bounded by x = y², the line x = 1 and the x-axis (with y ≥ 0) is revolved about the y-axis. Find the volume. Show your working.
questions.concept: Washer method in y about the y-axis
questions.why:
The axis is the y-axis, so integrate in y. At height y the region runs from the parabola x = y² out to the line x = 1, so the far boundary gives R(y) = 1 (constant) and the near boundary gives r(y) = y². The curves meet where y² = 1, so y runs from 0 to 1. V = π∫₀¹[1² − (y²)²]dy = π∫₀¹(1 − y⁴)dy = π[y − y⁵/5]₀¹ = π(1 − 1/5) = 4π/5.

Final answer: 4π/5 cubic units (also accepted: 0.8π or 2.51). A correct answer identifies R = 1, r = y², limits 0 to 1, and subtracts the squares. π∫(1 − y²)²dy = 8π/15 uses (R − r)² and is wrong; π∫₀¹(1 − y²)dy = 2π/3 forgets to square r.

questions.q: The region under y = x³, above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 1 is revolved about the y-axis. Use the shell method to find the volume. Show your working.
questions.concept: Shell method for a region under a curve
questions.why:
A vertical strip at position x has radius x (its distance from the y-axis) and height f(x) = x³. V = 2π∫₀¹x·x³dx = 2π∫₀¹x⁴dx = 2π[x⁵/5]₀¹ = 2π/5.

Final answer: 2π/5 cubic units (also accepted: 0.4π or 1.26). The working must show the integrand x·f(x) = x⁴, the coefficient 2π and the evaluation at 1. π/5 uses π instead of 2π; 2π∫₀¹x³dx = π/2 forgets the radius x; 2π∫₀¹x·x⁶dx squares the height, which the shell formula never does.

questions.q: In the washer formula V = π∫ₐᵇ([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²)dx and the shell formula V = 2π∫ₐᵇ x f(x)dx, state what each of R(x), r(x), x and f(x) measures, and explain why one formula carries π and the other 2π.
questions.concept: Meaning of the radii and heights in the volume formulas
questions.why:
R(x) is the outer radius: the distance from the axis of revolution to the boundary farther from it. r(x) is the inner radius: the distance from the axis to the nearer boundary. In the shell formula x is the radius of the shell, its distance from the axis of revolution, and f(x) is the height of the vertical strip that sweeps out the shell. The π in the washer formula comes from the area of a circular cross-section, πR² − πr² for an annulus, which is then integrated along the axis. The 2π in the shell formula comes from unrolling the cylindrical shell into a rectangle of length 2π × radius (the circumference) and height f(x), so the integrand is circumference × height with no square anywhere.

A correct answer names outer radius, inner radius, shell radius and strip height, and links π to the area of a circle and 2π to the circumference.

checks.topic:
Faraday's law and Lenz's law as concepts.

Covers what the flux rule actually asserts: only a changing magnetic flux Φ_B = BA cos θ induces an emf, never the flux itself. And the meaning of θ as the angle from the loop's normal.

Covers the physical content of the minus sign: the induced current opposes the CHANGE in flux, not the external field.

With it, the deck's three working rules, and the right-hand grip rule for getting the sense of the current.

Ends on the energy argument, that Lenz's law is conservation of energy rather than a separate empirical law.

questions.q: An average emf of 6.0 V is induced in a 300-turn coil while the flux through each turn changes by 4.0 mWb. How long did the change take?
questions.concept: Rearranging Faraday's law for the time
questions.why:
ε = N ΔΦ/Δt, so Δt = N ΔΦ/ε = (300)(4.0 × 10⁻³)/6.0 = 1.2/6.0 = 0.20 s.

5.0 s is ε/(N ΔΦ), the ratio upside down; 6.7 × 10⁻⁴ s is ΔΦ/ε with N forgotten; 7.2 s multiplies N ΔΦ by the emf instead of dividing by it.

questions.q: A rectangular loop 20 cm by 15 cm lies in a uniform field of 0.40 T. The normal to the loop makes 60° with the field. What is the magnetic flux through the loop?
questions.concept: Flux through a rectangular loop with an inclined normal
questions.why:
A = (0.20)(0.15) = 0.030 m². The angle is already given from the normal, so Φ = BA cos θ = (0.40)(0.030) cos 60° = (0.012)(0.50) = 6.0 × 10⁻³ Wb.

1.2 × 10⁻² Wb is BA with the angle ignored; 1.0 × 10⁻² Wb uses cos 30°, treating 60° as the angle from the plane; 60 Wb leaves the sides in centimetres, giving an area 10⁴ times too big.

questions.q: A flat loop lies in the page. A uniform field directed into the page is switched on, rising from zero. As seen by the reader, in which sense does the induced current flow, and which way does its own field point inside the loop?
options: Anticlockwise; induced field out of the page
Clockwise; induced field into the page
Clockwise; induced field out of the page
Anticlockwise; induced field into the page
questions.concept: Lenz's law with the right-hand grip rule
questions.why:
Step 1: the external flux is into the page and increasing, so the induced field inside the loop must oppose the increase by pointing out of the page. Step 2: grip rule, thumb out of the page, fingers curl anticlockwise, so the current is anticlockwise.

'Clockwise; into the page' makes the induced field aid the growing flux, which is the answer for a decreasing field; the other two pair a sense with the field it does not produce, the grip rule applied backwards.

questions.q: A 200-turn coil of area 1.0 × 10⁻² m² is placed so that its plane is parallel to a uniform field. The field rises at a steady 50 T/s. What is the induced emf?
questions.concept: Changing field with zero flux
questions.why:
Plane parallel to B means the normal is at 90° to B, so Φ = BA cos 90° = 0 at every instant. Since Φ never changes, dΦ/dt = 0 and ε = 0, however fast B rises. A changing field is not the same as a changing flux.

100 V is NA dB/dt with cos θ = 1, treating the coil as face-on; 0.50 V is the same with N forgotten; 50 V quotes the rate of change of B as if it were a voltage.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.80 m moves at right angles to a uniform field of 0.50 T and to its own length. What speed is needed for an emf of 0.20 V between its ends?
questions.concept: Rearranging the motional emf formula
questions.why:
ε = BLv, so v = ε/(BL) = 0.20/((0.50)(0.80)) = 0.20/0.40 = 0.50 m/s.

0.40 m/s divides by B only and forgets L; 2.0 m/s is BL/ε, the ratio inverted; 0.080 m/s multiplies ε by BL instead of dividing.

questions.q: An a.c. generator delivers an rms emf of 120 V. What is its peak emf?
questions.concept: Peak emf from rms emf
questions.why:
ε_rms = ε_peak/√2, so ε_peak = √2 × 120 = 1.414 × 120 = 170 V (169.7 V).

85 V divides by √2 instead of multiplying; 240 V doubles instead of multiplying by √2; 120 V treats rms and peak as the same number.

questions.q: A 50-turn coil of area 2.0 × 10⁻² m² has its normal at 60° to a uniform field that rises at a steady 3.0 T/s. What is the induced emf?
questions.concept: Faraday's law for an inclined coil
questions.why:
Only B changes, so ε = N A cos θ dB/dt = (50)(2.0 × 10⁻²)(cos 60°)(3.0) = (50)(2.0 × 10⁻²)(0.50)(3.0) = 1.5 V.

3.0 V ignores the angle; 2.6 V uses cos 30°, measuring the angle from the plane; 0.030 V forgets N.

questions.q: A bar magnet is held perfectly still with its north pole deep inside a closed coil. Which pair correctly describes the flux through the coil and the emf induced in it?
questions.concept: Flux versus rate of change of flux
questions.why:
The magnet's field threads the coil, so the flux is large. But ε = −N dΦ/dt depends on the rate of change of flux, and a stationary magnet gives a constant flux, so the emf is zero. Faraday's conclusion: the existence of flux is not sufficient; the flux must be changing.

'Large flux, large emf' mistakes flux for its rate of change; 'zero flux' is wrong because a magnet inside a coil certainly threads it with field lines; the zero emf is right but the reason offered is wrong.

questions.q: A flexible loop of 5 turns lies with its normal parallel to a uniform field of 0.60 T. The loop is squeezed so that its area shrinks at a steady 0.020 m²/s. Calculate the induced emf. State the emf if instead the loop is held rigid while the field is kept steady at 1.2 T. Show your working.
questions.concept: Emf from a changing area
questions.why:
With B and θ fixed, Φ = BA and dΦ/dt = B dA/dt. So ε = N B dA/dt = (5)(0.60)(0.020) = 0.060 V. If the loop is rigid and B is steady, nothing in Φ = BA cos θ changes, so ε = 0, however large the field.

Final answer: 0.060 V (accept 0.058 to 0.062), and 0 V for the rigid loop in a steady field. A correct answer uses the rate of change of area, multiplies by N and B, and says that a steady flux induces nothing. 0.012 V forgot N; 0.12 V for the second part treats the larger field as if it were a change.

questions.q: The flux through each turn of a 20-turn coil varies with time as Φ = 0.30t² Wb, with t in seconds. Calculate the induced emf at t = 2.0 s, and find the time at which the emf is 6.0 V. Show your working.
questions.concept: Instantaneous emf from a time-dependent flux
questions.why:
Differentiate: dΦ/dt = 0.60t Wb/s, so |ε| = N dΦ/dt = 20 × 0.60t = 12t volts. At t = 2.0 s: ε = 12 × 2.0 = 24 V. For ε = 6.0 V: 12t = 6.0, so t = 0.50 s.

Final answer: 24 V at t = 2.0 s (accept 23.5 to 24.5) and t = 0.50 s. A correct answer differentiates before substituting and multiplies by N. 1.2 V at t = 2.0 s is Φ itself (0.30 × 4) with no differentiation; 1.2 V or 2.4 V forgets N; substituting t = 6 gives nonsense.

questions.q: An 80-turn coil of area 5.0 × 10⁻³ m² sits face-on to a uniform field of 0.25 T, so that its normal is along the field. It is turned through 90° in 0.10 s so that its plane now contains the field. Calculate the average emf induced. Show your working.
questions.concept: Average emf from turning a coil through a right angle
questions.why:
Initial flux per turn: Φ₁ = BA cos 0° = (0.25)(5.0 × 10⁻³) = 1.25 × 10⁻³ Wb. Final flux: Φ₂ = BA cos 90° = 0. So |ΔΦ| = 1.25 × 10⁻³ Wb and ε_av = N |ΔΦ|/Δt = (80)(1.25 × 10⁻³)/(0.10) = 0.10/0.10 = 1.0 V.

Final answer: 1.0 V (accept 0.98 to 1.02). A correct answer states the initial flux BA, the final flux zero, and divides N ΔΦ by 0.10 s; it may note that this is an average, since the flux does not fall uniformly. 0.0125 V forgot N; 2.0 V used a flux change of 2BA, which is a full flip through 180°, not a quarter turn.

questions.q: A bar magnet is pushed north-pole-first into a coil connected to a centre-zero galvanometer, held still inside for a moment, then pulled out again. Describe what the galvanometer shows during each of the three stages and explain each reading using Faraday's law and Lenz's law.
questions.concept: Faraday's magnet-and-coil experiment explained
questions.why:
Stage 1, pushing in: the flux through the coil increases, so by Faraday's law an emf is induced and the needle deflects, say to the left. By Lenz's law the current makes the near face a north pole, opposing the approach. Stage 2, held still: the flux is large but constant, so dΦ/dt = 0, the emf is zero and the needle returns to the centre, even though the magnet is inside the coil. Stage 3, pulling out: the flux decreases, so an emf is induced again but the current reverses, the near face becomes a south pole to hold the magnet back, and the needle deflects the other way.

A correct answer gives deflection, zero, opposite deflection, ties each to the flux increasing, constant, decreasing, and names the pole on the near face or the reversal of current as Lenz's law.

checks.topic:
The concepts of both Week 11 decks.

Decomposition versus modularisation. Module independence measured by cohesion and coupling. The single responsibility principle. Information hiding and its benefits. Refactoring. Horizontal versus vertical structural partitioning.

From the second deck: the definition and purpose of software architecture, the three levels of software pattern (architectural, design, idiom), and the two generic design approaches.

Questions target the precise wording of the definitions, and the mechanism behind each claim, rather than recognition of the vocabulary.

questions.q: Orders calls Payments.charge(), Stock.reserve() and Email.send(). Stock calls Email.send(). Payments and Email call nothing outside themselves. Measuring coupling as the number of other modules a module depends on, what are the counts for Orders and for Stock?
questions.concept: Counting coupling from a call list
questions.why:
Coupling is the extent to which a module depends on other modules before performing its function. Orders cannot place an order without Payments, Stock and Email: 3. Stock cannot reserve without Email: 1. Payments and Email depend on nothing: 0 each.

Orders 3, Stock 0 misses the Stock to Email call; Orders 2, Stock 1 drops Email from Orders because Stock already uses it, but a shared dependency still counts for each module that has it; Orders 4, Stock 2 counts each module as depending on itself.

questions.q: Three notes from a design meeting: (i) 'the system is split into a client layer, a service layer and a database layer'; (ii) 'a component notifies each of its subscribers whenever its state changes'; (iii) 'in C, always test the value returned by malloc before using it'. Classify each as an architectural pattern, a design pattern or an idiom.
questions.concept: Classifying pattern levels
questions.why:
Architectural patterns are high-level: the overall structure and its subsystems, so the three layers are (i). Design patterns are medium-level: component-to-component interaction mechanisms, so the subscriber notification is (ii). Idioms are low-level and programming-language specific, so the C rule about malloc is (iii).

The second option swaps the top two levels; the third calls a language-independent interaction rule an idiom and a C-specific rule a design pattern; the fourth reverses the whole scale.

questions.q: Put the steps of top-down design in order. A: treat each sub-system as a system and decompose it further. B: take the whole software system as one entity. C: compose all the components so the whole system comes into existence. D: decompose it into sub-systems based on some characteristic. E: stop when the lowest level of the hierarchy is reached.
questions.concept: Ordering the top-down design steps
questions.why:
Top-down starts with the whole system as one entity (B), decomposes it into sub-systems (D), treats each sub-system as a system and decomposes further (A), keeps going until the lowest level is reached (E), and only then, when all components are composed, does the whole system come into existence (C).

B, A, D, E, C tries to decompose a sub-system before any sub-system exists; C, B, D, A, E composes first, which is bottom-up thinking; B, D, E, A, C stops at the lowest level before the further decomposition that reaches it.

questions.q: Design P: the top module decides which of three reports to produce and does nothing else; the modules beneath it read the file, compute the totals and print. Design Q: a control module runs four functions in turn, handing the output of each to the next. Which partitioning is each?
questions.concept: Identifying horizontal versus vertical partitioning
questions.why:
In vertical partitioning the top-level control modules do the decision-making and little processing, while the low-level worker modules do all the input, computation and output: that is P. In horizontal partitioning control modules are used to communicate between functions and execute them, passing data across the interfaces as it moves from one function to the next: that is Q.

Swapping them mistakes 'passes data between functions' for decision-making; 'both vertical' misses that Q's controller is a data conduit, not a decider; 'both horizontal' misses that P's controller does nothing but choose.

questions.q: A reporting system is built bottom-up: file-reading and string primitives are composed into a Parser, the Parser and a database primitive into a ReportService, and the ReportService with a Scheduler into the complete system. Which level has the greatest abstraction and which the least?
options: Greatest: the primitives; least: the complete system
Greatest: the complete system; least: the primitives
Greatest: the Parser; least: the ReportService
They are all at the same level of abstraction
questions.concept: Abstraction levels in bottom-up composition
questions.why:
Bottom-up design starts with the most specific and basic components and composes higher-level components from them; with each higher level the amount of abstraction is increased. The primitives are the most specific, and the single component at the top, the complete system, is the most abstract.

The first option reverses the direction; the third picks two middle levels and puts the lower one above the higher; the fourth denies that abstraction changes with level, which is the rule this design relies on.

questions.q: A validate_email() function written for the registration module is later called, unchanged, by the password-reset module and by a separate marketing program. Which listed advantage of modularisation is this?
options: Smaller modules are easier and faster to test
Large programs can be written by several people
Modules and functions can be used in other parts of the program or in another program
Understanding a small function is easier
questions.concept: Matching an outcome to an advantage of modularisation
questions.why:
The function is being used both in another part of the same program (password reset) and in another program (marketing). That is exactly the reuse advantage: modules and functions can be used in other parts of the program or in another program.

Easier testing and easier understanding are about the size of the unit, not about where it is used; several people writing a program is about dividing the work, and nothing in the case mentions who wrote what.

questions.q: Component X performs four functions that have a limited relationship with one another. Component Y performs three functions that all serve one aim. The refactoring prescribed for low cohesion is applied to this design. How many components exist afterwards?
questions.concept: Applying the refactoring prescription
questions.why:
The prescription is to refactor a low-cohesion component into as many components as it has unrelated functions, each exhibiting high cohesion. X becomes 4 components. Y is already highly cohesive, so it is left alone: 4 + 1 = 5.

4 forgets Y; 7 splits Y as well, though its functions work together; 2 leaves X in one piece, which is the design the refactoring was meant to fix.

questions.q: Module Reports reads the internal list Orders.pending directly, instead of calling the function Orders.count_pending() that Orders provides. Which design rule does Reports break?
questions.concept: Information hiding
questions.why:
Information hiding requires that the data structures and processing details of one module are not accessible to other modules; they pass each other only the information required to accomplish the function. Reports is reaching into Orders' data structure instead of using the controlled interface.

The single responsibility principle is about a module doing one job, and Reports may well do only reporting; vertical partitioning is about who decides and who works in a hierarchy; top-down is a design approach, not a rule about access.

questions.q: An online exam application needs a 'submit attempt' feature. Decompose it into at least three subproblems. Then take those subproblems together with 'edit profile' and 'change password' and group them into modules: name each module, list what it holds, and state which of your two steps was decomposition and which was modularisation. Show your working.
questions.concept: Decomposing a feature into subproblems and modules
questions.why:
Decomposition breaks the feature into smaller subproblems, for example: validate the submitted answers, save the attempt, compute the score, notify the student of the result. Modularisation groups related subproblems into independent modules, each with everything it needs for its part: an Attempt module (validate answers, save the attempt), a Grading module (compute the score), a Notification module (notify the student), and an Account module (edit profile, change password), since those two concern the user's account and not the exam.

A correct answer lists three or more sensible subproblems of submitting an attempt, groups them so that each module has one aim and the account tasks sit apart from the exam tasks, and says that breaking the feature apart is decomposition and grouping into modules is modularisation. Any grouping that puts 'change password' inside the grading or attempt module is low cohesion and is not accepted.

questions.q: A car carries passengers from one place to another. Using its brake, radiator, battery and steering wheel: give one example of high cohesion inside a single part, one example of low coupling between two parts, and one design change that would raise the coupling between two parts. Show your working.
questions.concept: Cohesion and coupling in the car analogy
questions.why:
High cohesion: every element of the brake (pedal, lines, pads, discs) works towards the one aim of stopping the car, and nothing in it serves any other purpose. Low coupling: the radiator and the steering wheel do not depend on each other at all; the radiator meets the rest of the car only through its hoses, so it can be replaced without touching the steering. Raising coupling: wiring the brake so that it works only while the radiator fan is running would make braking depend on cooling, so a fault or change in the radiator would now affect the brake.

A correct answer judges cohesion inside one part (all its elements serve one aim), judges coupling between two parts (one can be changed without the other), and proposes a change that makes one part depend on another. Naming the battery as the low-coupling example is fine only if it is the connection, not the battery's own parts, that is discussed.

questions.q: A library app has three components: Catalogue (stores the books), Loans (records who has borrowed what) and Notifier (sends reminders). Write out its software architecture using the three parts of the definition: the components, the attributes (properties) of each, and the relationships between them. Show your working.
questions.concept: Describing a software architecture
questions.why:
Software architecture is the structure of the system: its components, the attributes of those components, and the relationships between them. Components: Catalogue, Loans, Notifier. Attributes: Catalogue holds the list of books and their availability; Loans holds the record of borrower, book and due date; Notifier holds the message templates and the sending channel. Relationships: Loans asks Catalogue whether a book is available and tells it when a book goes out or comes back; Loans asks Notifier to send a reminder when a due date passes; Notifier does not depend on Catalogue.

A correct answer names the three components, gives at least one property for each, and states the direction of at least two dependencies between them. Listing components alone, with no attributes or relationships, is only one third of the definition and is not accepted.

questions.q: Top-down and bottom-up design are described as not individually practicable, so that a combination is used. Explain what goes wrong if a team uses only top-down, what goes wrong if it uses only bottom-up, and what a combination looks like for a new inventory system built on an existing database library.
questions.concept: Combining top-down and bottom-up design
questions.why:
Top-down alone decomposes the whole system into sub-systems on assumptions about what the lowest level will look like, and may arrive at a bottom level that does not match any component that can actually be built or reused. Bottom-up alone composes higher components from existing primitives with no guarantee that what they add up to is the system that was wanted. In the combination, the inventory system is decomposed top-down from the whole into stock, orders and reporting sub-systems because it is being designed from scratch with details unknown, while the data-access parts are built bottom-up from the existing database library because those primitives already exist and can be reused.

A correct answer gives a failure for each approach used alone, and matches top-down to the new, unknown parts and bottom-up to the existing library in the example.

checks.topic:
Problems-only session on Week 11 volumes of revolution.

Set up and evaluate π∫ₐᵇ[R]²dx, π∫ₐᵇ([R]² − [r]²)dx and 2π∫ₐᵇ x f(x)dx on the deck's own numbers.

Her six worked examples. Then all three unanswered TASKs: √x from 1 to 4; y = x² over [0,2] about y = −1; and y = x against y = x² about the y-axis.

Plus irrational limits (√2, √3), a shifted axis, and one solid computed twice as a cross-check.

questions.q: The region between the parabola x = y² + 1 and the line x = 4 is revolved about the line x = 4. Find the volume.
questions.concept: Disc method in y about a vertical line
questions.why:
The axis is x = 4, so the radius is the horizontal distance from the line to the parabola: R(y) = 4 − (y² + 1) = 3 − y². Limits: y² + 1 = 4 gives y = ±√3. V = π∫₋√₃^√₃(3 − y²)²dy = π∫₋√₃^√₃(9 − 6y² + y⁴)dy = π[9y − 2y³ + y⁵/5]₋√₃^√₃. Using (√3)³ = 3√3 and (√3)⁵ = 9√3, the bracket at √3 is 9√3 − 6√3 + 9√3/5 = 24√3/5; the integrand is even, so V = 2π(24√3/5) = 48√3π/5 cubic units (≈ 52.2).

24√3π/5 evaluates at the upper limit only and forgets that the lower limit contributes the same again; 36√3π/5 takes (√3)⁵ as 3√3; 4√3π forgets to square the radius.

questions.q: The region between y = x² and y = x³ for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume.
questions.concept: Washer with two curved boundaries
questions.why:
On [0, 1], x² ≥ x³, so R(x) = x² and r(x) = x³. V = π∫₀¹[(x²)² − (x³)²]dx = π∫₀¹(x⁴ − x⁶)dx = π[x⁵/5 − x⁷/7]₀¹ = π(1/5 − 1/7) = π(7 − 5)/35 = 2π/35 cubic units.

π/105 integrates (x² − x³)², the difference squared; 12π/35 adds 1/5 and 1/7 instead of subtracting; π/12 forgets to square the radii, π∫(x² − x³)dx.

questions.q: The region enclosed by the curve y = 4 − x² and the x-axis is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume.
questions.concept: Disc method with limits from the roots
questions.why:
Limits: 4 − x² = 0 gives x = −2 and x = 2. R(x) = 4 − x², so V = π∫₋₂²(4 − x²)²dx = π∫₋₂²(16 − 8x² + x⁴)dx = π[16x − 8x³/3 + x⁵/5]₋₂². At x = 2 the bracket is 32 − 64/3 + 32/5 = (480 − 320 + 96)/15 = 256/15, and the even integrand doubles it: V = 512π/15 cubic units (≈ 107.2).

256π/15 integrates from 0 to 2 only; 32π/3 forgets to square the radius; 128π/15 has the sign of the x⁵/5 term wrong, 32 − 64/3 − 32/5.

questions.q: The region enclosed by y = 3x and y = x² is revolved about the y-axis. Use the shell method to find the volume.
questions.concept: Shell method for a region between two curves
questions.why:
Limits: 3x = x² gives x(x − 3) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 3. On (0, 3) the line is on top (at x = 1: 3 > 1), so the strip height is 3x − x² and its radius is x. V = 2π∫₀³x(3x − x²)dx = 2π∫₀³(3x² − x³)dx = 2π[x³ − x⁴/4]₀³ = 2π(27 − 81/4) = 2π(27/4) = 27π/2 cubic units.

27π/4 uses π instead of 2π; 9π leaves out the radius x, 2π∫(3x − x²)dx; −27π/2 takes the height as x² − 3x, bottom minus top.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x³, the y-axis and the line y = 8 is revolved about the y-axis. Find the volume.
questions.concept: Disc method in y after inverting the curve
questions.why:
The axis is the y-axis, so write the curve as x = y^(1/3); the radius at height y is R(y) = y^(1/3) and y runs from 0 to 8. V = π∫₀⁸(y^(1/3))²dy = π∫₀⁸y^(2/3)dy = π[3y^(5/3)/5]₀⁸ = π(3/5)(8^(5/3)) = π(3/5)(32) = 96π/5 cubic units (≈ 60.3).

12π integrates y^(1/3) without squaring it, π(3/4)(16); 128π/7 is π∫₀²(x³)²dx, the volume about the x-axis instead; 32π forgets the factor 3/5 from integrating y^(2/3).

questions.q: The region under y = x², above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 1 is revolved about the line y = −1. Find the volume.
questions.concept: Washer about a shifted horizontal axis
questions.why:
Radii are distances from y = −1: R(x) = x² − (−1) = x² + 1 and r(x) = 0 − (−1) = 1. V = π∫₀¹[(x² + 1)² − 1²]dx = π∫₀¹(x⁴ + 2x² + 1 − 1)dx = π∫₀¹(x⁴ + 2x²)dx = π[x⁵/5 + 2x³/3]₀¹ = π(1/5 + 2/3) = 13π/15 cubic units.

π/5 ignores the shift and rotates about the x-axis; 28π/15 shifts the outer radius but leaves r = 0, filling a hole that is there; −7π/15 shifts the wrong way, using R = x² − 1.

questions.q: The region under y = x², above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 2 is revolved about the y-axis. Use the washer method, integrating in y, to find the volume.
questions.concept: Washer in y with the inner radius from the inverted curve
questions.why:
At height y the region runs from the curve x = √y out to the line x = 2, so R(y) = 2 and r(y) = √y, with y from 0 to 4 (the curve reaches y = 2² = 4). V = π∫₀⁴[2² − (√y)²]dy = π∫₀⁴(4 − y)dy = π[4y − y²/2]₀⁴ = π(16 − 8) = 8π cubic units. The shell method gives the same: 2π∫₀²x·x²dx = 2π(4) = 8π.

16π forgets to subtract the inner radius; 8π/3 integrates (2 − √y)², the difference squared; −8π swaps the two radii.

questions.q: The region between y = x² and y = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 is revolved about the x-axis. A student writes V = π∫₀²(2x − x²)²dx. Which single error has been made?
options: (R − r)² has been used in place of R² − r²
R and r have been swapped
questions.concept: Why the washer subtracts squares
questions.why:
The cross-section is an annulus of area πR² − πr², so the integrand must be R² − r² = (2x)² − (x²)² = 4x² − x⁴, giving 64π/15. Squaring the difference gives (2x − x²)² = 4x² − 4x³ + x⁴, a different and smaller integrand, giving 16π/15.

The limits 0 and 2 are right (the curves meet at x = 0 and x = 2); π is correct for a washer; 2x ≥ x² on [0, 2], so R = 2x and r = x² are in the right order.

questions.q: The region under y = x², above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 1 is revolved about the line y = 1. Find the volume. Show your working.
questions.concept: Washer about an axis above the region
questions.why:
Radii are distances from the line y = 1. The boundary farther from that line is the x-axis, at distance 1 − 0 = 1, so R(x) = 1; the nearer boundary is the curve, at distance 1 − x², so r(x) = 1 − x². V = π∫₀¹[1² − (1 − x²)²]dx = π∫₀¹[1 − (1 − 2x² + x⁴)]dx = π∫₀¹(2x² − x⁴)dx = π[2x³/3 − x⁵/5]₀¹ = π(2/3 − 1/5) = 7π/15.

Final answer: 7π/15 cubic units (also accepted: 1.47). A correct answer identifies R = 1 and r = 1 − x² as distances from y = 1, subtracts the squares and evaluates. π∫₀¹(x² + 1)²dx − π = 13π/15 shifts the wrong way (that is the solid about y = −1); π∫x⁴dx = π/5 ignores the shift.

questions.q: The region under y = x, above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 1 is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume by the shell method (integrating in y), then confirm it by the disc method. Show your working.
questions.concept: Cross-checking a volume by two methods
questions.why:
Shells: the axis is the x-axis, so the strips are horizontal at height y, with radius y. The strip runs from the line x = y to the edge x = 1, so its length is f(y) = 1 − y, and y runs from 0 to 1. V = 2π∫₀¹y(1 − y)dy = 2π∫₀¹(y − y²)dy = 2π[y²/2 − y³/3]₀¹ = 2π(1/2 − 1/3) = 2π(1/6) = π/3. Discs: R(x) = x, so V = π∫₀¹x²dx = π[x³/3]₀¹ = π/3. The two agree, as they must, since they measure the same cone.

Final answer: π/3 cubic units by both methods (also accepted: 1.05). The working must show f(y) = 1 − y, the 2π, and the disc integral π∫x²dx. 2π∫₀¹y·y dy = 2π/3 takes the strip length as y instead of 1 − y and is wrong.

questions.q: The region enclosed by y = x² and y = x + 2 is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume. Show your working.
questions.concept: Washer with limits from the intersection of two curves
questions.why:
Boundaries: x² = x + 2 gives x² − x − 2 = (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0, so x = −1 and x = 2. On (−1, 2) the line is farther from the x-axis (at x = 0: 2 > 0), so R(x) = x + 2 and r(x) = x². V = π∫₋₁²[(x + 2)² − (x²)²]dx = π∫₋₁²(x² + 4x + 4 − x⁴)dx = π[x³/3 + 2x² + 4x − x⁵/5]₋₁². At x = 2 the bracket is 8/3 + 8 + 8 − 32/5 = 184/15; at x = −1 it is −1/3 + 2 − 4 + 1/5 = −32/15. V = π(184/15 + 32/15) = 216π/15 = 72π/5.

Final answer: 72π/5 cubic units (also accepted: 14.4π or 45.2). A correct answer finds the limits by solving x² = x + 2, identifies R = x + 2 and r = x², subtracts the squares and evaluates at both limits, remembering that subtracting −32/15 adds. π(184/15 − 32/15) = 152π/15 has that sign wrong; using (x + 2 − x²)² as the integrand squares the difference and is wrong.

questions.q: The region under y = x (0 ≤ x ≤ 1, above the x-axis) is revolved about the y-axis. A student writes V = π∫₀¹x²dx = π/3. Explain what solid that integral really measures, and set up a correct integral.
questions.concept: Matching the formula to the axis of revolution
questions.why:
π∫ₐᵇ[f(x)]²dx is the disc formula for revolution about the x-axis: it stacks discs of radius f(x) = x along the x-axis, so π/3 is the volume of the cone made by spinning the region about the x-axis, not the y-axis. For the y-axis, either integrate along that axis with washers in y, where at height y the region runs from x = y to x = 1, giving V = π∫₀¹(1² − y²)dy = 2π/3, or use shells in x with radius x and height x, giving V = 2π∫₀¹x·x dx = 2π/3. Both give 2π/3, which is not π/3.

A correct answer says the student's integral is the disc formula about the x-axis, and gives either π∫₀¹(1 − y²)dy or 2π∫₀¹x²dx (value 2π/3) for the y-axis.

checks.topic:
The same Faraday/Lenz material worked numerically.

Computing induced emf from a rate of change of B in an N-turn coil.

Evaluating Φ = BA cos θ when the question specifies the angle to the loop's PLANE.

Motional emf ε = BLv, with its induced current I = ε/R and retarding force F = B²L²v/R.

Also generator output: ε_peak = NBAω with ω = 2πf, and ε_rms = ε_peak/√2.

And the time-independent circulated charge q = N|ΔΦ|/R.

Emphasis throughout on the unit, angle, 2π and current-sense traps.

questions.q: A 120-turn circular coil of diameter 6.0 cm and total resistance 1.5 Ω has its plane perpendicular to a uniform field that rises at a steady 2.5 T/s. What current flows in the coil?
questions.concept: Induced current from a rate of change of B
questions.why:
Radius 3.0 cm = 0.030 m, so A = π(0.030)² = 2.83 × 10⁻³ m². Plane perpendicular to B means θ = 0. ε = NA dB/dt = (120)(2.83 × 10⁻³)(2.5) = 0.848 V, and I = ε/R = 0.848/1.5 = 0.57 A.

0.85 A is the emf quoted as a current, R never used; 2.3 A uses the 6.0 cm diameter as the radius, four times the area; 4.7 × 10⁻³ A forgets N.

questions.q: A 25-turn square coil of side 12 cm sits in a uniform field of 0.60 T with the plane of the coil at 40° to the field. What is the flux linkage NΦ?
questions.concept: Flux linkage with the angle given to the plane
questions.why:
The plane is at 40° to B, so the normal is at 90° − 40° = 50°. A = (0.12)² = 1.44 × 10⁻² m². Φ = BA cos 50° = (0.60)(1.44 × 10⁻²)(0.643) = 5.55 × 10⁻³ Wb per turn, and NΦ = 25 × 5.55 × 10⁻³ = 0.139 Wb, about 0.14 Wb.

0.17 Wb uses cos 40°, the angle from the plane; 0.22 Wb is NBA with the angle ignored; 5.6 × 10⁻³ Wb is the flux through one turn, N forgotten.

questions.q: A rod sliding on rails in a uniform field needs an applied force of 0.30 N to keep it moving at a steady 2.0 m/s against the induced current's retarding force. If it is instead kept moving at 6.0 m/s, what force is needed and what mechanical power is supplied?
questions.concept: Scaling of retarding force and power with speed
questions.why:
F = B²L²v/R is proportional to v, so tripling the speed triples the force: F = 3 × 0.30 = 0.90 N. Power P = Fv = (0.90)(6.0) = 5.4 W, nine times the original 0.60 W, because P = B²L²v²/R goes as v².

'0.90 N and 1.8 W' scales the power with v instead of v²; '2.7 N and 16 W' scales the force with v² instead of v; '0.30 N and 1.8 W' assumes the force does not depend on speed at all.

questions.q: A coil of 250 turns and area 0.012 m² rotates at 1200 revolutions per minute in a uniform field of 0.30 T, about an axis perpendicular to the field. What rms emf does it deliver?
questions.concept: Rms emf of a generator from its rotation rate
questions.why:
f = 1200/60 = 20 Hz, so ω = 2πf = 125.7 rad/s. ε_peak = NBAω = (250)(0.30)(0.012)(125.7) = 113 V. ε_rms = ε_peak/√2 = 113/1.414 = 80 V.

18 V uses f = 20 in place of ω, missing the 2π; 113 V is the peak, not the rms; 1.1 × 10³ V uses 1200 rev/min directly as ω.

questions.q: An 80-turn coil of area 3.0 × 10⁻³ m² and total resistance 4.0 Ω starts face-on to a uniform field of 0.50 T and is flipped right over (through 180°) in 0.10 s. How much charge circulates?
questions.concept: Charge circulated when a coil is flipped
questions.why:
Flipping reverses the flux from +BA to −BA, so |ΔΦ| = 2BA = 2(0.50)(3.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.0 × 10⁻³ Wb. q = N|ΔΦ|/R = (80)(3.0 × 10⁻³)/4.0 = 0.24/4.0 = 0.060 C. The 0.10 s plays no part.

0.030 C uses ΔΦ = BA, forgetting that a flip doubles the change; 0.60 C is the average current (0.24/0.10/4.0) reported as a charge; 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ C forgets N.

questions.q: A generator coil has a peak emf of 60 V. What is the instantaneous emf at the moment when the normal to the coil makes 30° with the field?
questions.concept: Instantaneous emf of a rotating coil
questions.why:
Φ = BA cos ωt gives ε = ε_peak sin ωt, and ωt is the angle between the normal and B. So ε = 60 sin 30° = 60 × 0.50 = 30 V.

52 V uses cos 30°, which is the flux's factor, not the emf's; 60 V assumes the emf is at its peak, which happens at 90°, when the flux is zero; 42 V is the rms value, which is not an instantaneous emf at all.

questions.q: A rod slides along horizontal rails so that the area enclosed by the circuit is decreasing. The uniform field is directed into the page. As seen by the reader, the induced current in the circuit is:
options: Anticlockwise; the induced field points out of the page
Anticlockwise; the induced field points into the page
Clockwise; the induced field points into the page
Zero; the field itself is not changing
questions.concept: Current sense for a rod on rails
questions.why:
The flux into the page is decreasing because the area is shrinking, so the induced field inside the loop must replace what is being lost: it points into the page. Grip rule, thumb into the page: the current is clockwise.

'Anticlockwise; out of the page' is the answer for an increasing area, opposing the field rather than the change; 'anticlockwise; into the page' has the grip rule backwards; 'zero' forgets that changing area changes flux just as well as changing B does.

questions.q: A conducting rod moves at steady speed across a uniform field, but the rails it rests on are not connected to each other, so the circuit is open. Which of the following are non-zero?
questions.concept: Emf without a closed circuit
questions.why:
The motional emf BLv exists across the rod's ends whether or not the circuit is closed: charges are pushed to the ends until their electric field balances the magnetic push. With no closed path there is no current, and with no current there is no magnetic force BIL on the rod, so it slides freely.

'Emf and current' needs a closed circuit; 'current and retarding force' both need current; 'none' forgets that the emf is there regardless, and would light nothing only because nothing is connected.

questions.q: A 120-turn coil of area 6.0 × 10⁻³ m², resistance 4.0 Ω, has its normal along a uniform field that falls steadily from 0.80 T to 0.20 T in 0.30 s. Calculate the emf, the current and the charge that circulates, and give the direction of the induced field inside the coil relative to the original field. Show your working.
questions.concept: Faraday's law chained to current, charge and direction
questions.why:
|ΔΦ| = ΔB × A = (0.80 − 0.20)(6.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.6 × 10⁻³ Wb per turn; N|ΔΦ| = 120 × 3.6 × 10⁻³ = 0.432 Wb. ε = N|ΔΦ|/Δt = 0.432/0.30 = 1.44 V. I = ε/R = 1.44/4.0 = 0.36 A. q = N|ΔΦ|/R = 0.432/4.0 = 0.108 C (check: I × Δt = 0.36 × 0.30 = 0.108 C, equal because the rate is uniform). The flux is decreasing, so by Lenz's law the induced field inside the coil points in the same direction as the original field, to maintain the flux being lost.

Final answer: 1.4 V (accept 1.4 to 1.5), 0.36 A (accept 0.35 to 0.37), 0.11 C (accept 0.10 to 0.11), induced field along the original B. 'Opposite to B' is the answer for an increasing field and is wrong here; 0.012 V forgot N.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.60 m and mass 0.20 kg moves at 5.0 m/s on frictionless horizontal rails in a vertical 0.40 T field; circuit resistance 0.30 Ω. Calculate the emf, the current and the retarding force. The applied force is then removed; calculate the rod's initial deceleration. Show your working.
questions.concept: Retarding force and deceleration of a released rod
questions.why:
ε = BLv = (0.40)(0.60)(5.0) = 1.2 V. I = ε/R = 1.2/0.30 = 4.0 A. F = BIL = (0.40)(4.0)(0.60) = 0.96 N, directed against the motion (equivalently F = B²L²v/R = (0.16)(0.36)(5.0)/0.30 = 0.96 N). With no applied force this is the only horizontal force, so a = F/m = 0.96/0.20 = 4.8 m/s², slowing the rod. As v falls, F falls with it, so the deceleration shrinks and the rod slows exponentially rather than stopping dead.

Final answer: 1.2 V, 4.0 A, 0.96 N (accept 0.94 to 0.98), deceleration 4.8 m/s² (accept 4.7 to 4.9). A correct answer states that the force opposes the motion. 0.24 N used the emf as the current; 2.4 m/s² or 9.6 m/s² has a factor of 2 slip in F/m.

questions.q: A generator coil of area 0.040 m² is to give a peak emf of 100 V at 50 Hz in a uniform field of 0.20 T. Calculate the number of turns needed, the rms emf it will deliver, and the instantaneous emf at the moment the plane of the coil is parallel to the field. Show your working.
questions.concept: Designing a generator coil
questions.why:
ω = 2πf = 2π(50) = 314 rad/s. ε_peak = NBAω, so N = ε_peak/(BAω) = 100/((0.20)(0.040)(314)) = 100/2.51 = 39.8, so 40 turns. ε_rms = ε_peak/√2 = 100/1.414 = 70.7 V. When the plane of the coil is parallel to B the normal is at 90° to B, the flux is zero and passing through zero fastest, so ε = ε_peak sin 90° = 100 V.

Final answer: 40 turns (accept 39 to 40), 71 V (accept 70 to 71), 100 V. A correct answer converts f to ω with 2π, rounds N to a whole number, and recognises that plane parallel to B is the maximum-emf position, not zero. 250 turns used f in place of ω; 0 V for the last part confuses zero flux with zero emf.

questions.q: A generator produces a sinusoidal emf with a peak value of 100 V. A student writes that 'the average emf over one cycle is 70.7 V'. Explain what 70.7 V actually is, what the true average of the emf over a full cycle is, and why that average is useless for describing the output.
questions.concept: Peak, rms and average emf
questions.why:
70.7 V is the rms (root mean square) value, ε_peak/√2: the steady d.c. voltage that would deliver the same power to a resistor, and what an a.c. meter reads. It is not an average of the emf. The emf ε = ε_peak sin ωt spends half of each cycle positive and half negative, so its true average over a full cycle is zero. Zero is useless because it says nothing about how much power the generator can deliver; power depends on ε², which is positive throughout the cycle, and the rms value is exactly the square root of the mean of ε².

A correct answer identifies 70.7 V as rms, states the full-cycle average is zero because of the sign change, and says the rms is used because power depends on the square of the emf.

checks.topic:
The same Week 11 material applied to concrete design judgements rather than recalled.

You read short module listings and pseudocode. You decide whether a module is cohesive, what it is coupled to and why, which principle a design violates, and how to redraw the boundaries.

Scenarios cover judging cohesion from a function list, and spotting coupling through a shared data structure.

Then evaluating what a proposed refactor buys and costs, and checking a hierarchy against vertical partitioning.

Then choosing top-down or bottom-up for a given project, and deciding whether a change qualifies as refactoring at all.

questions.q:
Which module has the lowest cohesion?

```
module Cart:     add_item, remove_item, cart_total
module Auth:     login, logout, reset_password
module Helpers:  format_date, send_sms, compute_tax, resize_image
module Reports:  daily_sales, monthly_sales, export_csv
```
questions.concept: Judging cohesion from a function list
questions.why:
Cohesion is the extent to which the functions in a module work together towards one aim. Cart's three functions all manage the cart, Auth's all manage sign-in, Reports' all produce sales reports. Helpers' four functions (dates, SMS, tax, images) serve four unrelated aims, so it has the lowest cohesion.

Picking Cart, Auth or Reports mistakes 'has several functions' for low cohesion; the test is whether the functions share an aim, not how many there are.

questions.q:
Which line couples Orders to the internal data structure of Stock?

```
1 module Stock:
2     levels = {}                      # sku -> units
3     reserve(sku, n): levels[sku] = levels[sku] - n
4
5 module Orders:
6     place(sku, n):
7         if Stock.levels[sku] >= n:
8             Stock.reserve(sku, n)
```
questions.concept: Spotting coupling through a shared data structure
questions.why:
Line 7 reads Stock.levels directly, so Orders now depends on Stock keeping its stock in a dictionary indexed by sku. If Stock changes that structure, Orders breaks. Line 8 calls the function Stock provides, which is the controlled interface: Orders depends on Stock's function, not on its internals, so that is acceptable coupling.

Line 3 is Stock using its own data, which is normal; 'lines 7 and 8' treats every dependency as bad, but a module calling another's interface is how modules are meant to communicate.

questions.q: Four changes are proposed to a working compute_bill() function. Which one is a refactoring?
options: Split compute_bill into three smaller functions; every input still gives the same output
Add a student discount to compute_bill
Change compute_bill to round totals to the nearest naira
Make compute_bill reject negative quantities it previously accepted
questions.concept: Identifying a refactoring
questions.why:
Refactoring is modifying a software system to improve the internal structure of the design without changing its external behaviour. Splitting the function while every input gives the same output changes only the internal structure.

Adding a discount adds functionality; rounding changes the values returned; rejecting inputs that were accepted changes what the function does for some inputs. All three alter external behaviour, so none is refactoring.

questions.q:
Main is the top of the hierarchy. Which line breaks vertical partitioning?

```
1 module Main:
2     run():
3         rows = Input.read_rows()
4         total = 0
5         for r in rows: total = total + r.amount
6         Output.show(total)
7 module Input:  read_rows()
8 module Output: show(x)
```
options: Line 3: the control module calls Input
Line 5: the control module does the computation
Line 6: the control module calls Output
questions.concept: Checking a hierarchy against vertical partitioning
questions.why:
In vertical partitioning the top-level control modules do the decision-making and little processing, while the worker modules perform all input, computation and output. Line 5 has Main summing the amounts itself: computation in the control module. The fix is a worker such as Totals.sum(rows).

Lines 3 and 6 are the control module directing workers to do input and output, which is exactly its job; 'nothing' misses that Main is doing the arithmetic.

questions.q: Project P: a payroll system to be built from scratch, with the detailed requirements still unknown. Project Q: a dashboard to be assembled from an existing, tested library of chart and query primitives. Which design approach suits each?
questions.concept: Choosing top-down or bottom-up design
questions.why:
Top-down is more suitable when the solution needs to be designed from scratch and specific details are unknown: P. Bottom-up is more suitable when a system is created from an existing system whose basic primitives can be used in the newer one: Q.

Reversing them starts P from primitives it does not have and decomposes Q as if its library did not exist; 'both top-down' throws away Q's reusable primitives; 'both bottom-up' has nothing to compose P from.

questions.q: Module Marks keeps every student's scores in a table. Module Transcript needs one student's average. Which interface obeys 'pass only the information required to accomplish the function'?
options: `Marks.dump_all()`, returning a copy of every score
questions.concept: Choosing an interface that hides information
questions.why:
Transcript needs one number for one student. Marks.average(student_id) takes only the identifier and returns only that number; the table stays inside Marks, so it can be reorganised without touching Transcript.

Passing scores_table hands the internal structure across the interface, so Transcript must know its layout; reading Marks.table directly gives Transcript access to the data structure, which is what information hiding forbids; dump_all() returns far more than is required and exposes every score.

questions.q:
Users changes its internal list to a dictionary. How many of the other modules must be edited?

```
module Users:   list = []  (internal);  count()
module Login:   calls Users.count()
module Admin:   reads Users.list directly
module Report:  reads Users.list directly
module Mailer:  calls Users.count()
```
questions.concept: Effect of information hiding on change
questions.why:
Login and Mailer use only the interface count(), which Users can keep working however the data is stored, so they need no change. Admin and Report reach into the list directly, so when it becomes a dictionary their code breaks and must be edited: 2. This is the benefit of information hiding, restricting the effects of a change in one component on others.

4 assumes every module that uses Users must change; 0 assumes the change is invisible to everyone, forgetting the two direct readers; 1 miscounts the direct readers.

questions.q: Cohesion and coupling are the two measures of module independence. Where is each one judged?
options: Cohesion between modules; coupling inside a module
Cohesion inside a module; coupling between modules
questions.concept: Where cohesion and coupling are judged
questions.why:
Cohesion is the extent to which the functions in a module work together to achieve the aim of the module, so it is judged inside one module and should be high. Coupling is the extent to which modules depend on other modules before performing their function, so it is judged between modules and should be low.

The first option swaps them; the other two lose the distinction that one measure looks inward and the other outward.

questions.q:
Regroup the functions of this module into high-cohesion modules. Name each new module, list its functions, and state how many modules you end with. Show your working.

```
module UserTools:
    register, login, send_newsletter,
    generate_sales_report, reset_password, export_sales_csv
```
questions.concept: Redrawing module boundaries for cohesion
questions.why:
Sort the functions by the aim each serves. register, login and reset_password all manage a user's account. send_newsletter is marketing communication. generate_sales_report and export_sales_csv both produce sales output. So: Accounts (register, login, reset_password), Marketing (send_newsletter), SalesReports (generate_sales_report, export_sales_csv). Three modules, each with one aim, and the external behaviour of every function unchanged.

A correct answer produces three modules with those groupings, or a defensible variant such as merging the newsletter into a Communications module on its own; it must not leave sales reporting inside the account module. Names may differ. Two modules (accounts versus everything else) is not accepted, since 'everything else' still mixes marketing with reporting.

questions.q: A team proposes splitting Utils, which holds four unrelated functions, into four separate modules with one function each. State whether the program's external behaviour changes, three things the split buys, and two costs it may bring, taken from the disadvantages of modularisation. Show your working.
questions.concept: Costs and benefits of a refactor
questions.why:
External behaviour does not change: each function still takes the same inputs and produces the same outputs, so this is a refactoring. It buys easier integration, easier testing and easier maintenance of the components, because each module now has a single aim and can be changed or tested without dragging the other three along; it also makes each module easier to reuse elsewhere. The costs come from the disadvantages of modularisation: any two of longer execution time, larger storage size, longer compilation and loading time, more inter-module communication problems, and more initial design time.

A correct answer says behaviour is unchanged, gives three benefits of the kind above, and names two of the five listed disadvantages. Claiming the split makes the program faster is wrong; longer execution time is a listed cost.

questions.q:
This is a horizontal partition. Count how many times a value crosses a module interface, in or out, during one call of run(); list the crossings in order, then name the stated cost of horizontal partitioning that this shows. Show your working.

```
module Control:
    run():
        rows  = Reader.read()
        clean = Validator.check(rows)
        total = Summer.sum(clean)
        Printer.show(total)
```
questions.concept: Counting interface crossings in horizontal partitioning
questions.why:
Follow the data. 1: rows returned from Reader to Control. 2: rows passed from Control into Validator. 3: clean returned from Validator to Control. 4: clean passed into Summer. 5: total returned from Summer to Control. 6: total passed into Printer. Six crossings, and every piece of data passes through Control twice on its way from one worker to the next. That is the stated cost: horizontal partitioning requires the passing of more data across the module interfaces, which makes the control flow more complex, especially where data moves rapidly from one function to another.

Final answer: 6 crossings. Also accepted: 3 if the student counts each worker call as one exchange, provided the list is consistent and the cost is named correctly. A correct answer lists the crossings in order and names the extra data passing across interfaces as the cost.

questions.q: A team splits a 6,000-line program into forty files and reports that it is now modularised. Explain what is missing from that claim: what makes a module independent, and what test you would apply to each of the forty files to decide whether the program really has been modularised rather than merely decomposed.
questions.concept: Decomposition versus modularisation
questions.why:
Cutting the code into files is decomposition: the application has been broken into parts. Modularisation requires that each part be an independent module with everything it needs to implement only its part of the functionality. Independence is measured by cohesion and coupling: the functions in each file should work together towards one aim (high cohesion), and each file should depend as little as possible on other files before it can do its job (low coupling), with its data structures hidden behind a controlled interface. The test for each file: do all its functions serve one aim, and can it be changed or tested without editing the other files? Forty files that reach into each other's data structures are decomposed but not modularised.

A correct answer separates decomposition from modularisation, names independence with cohesion and coupling (information hiding is a bonus), and gives a concrete test per file.

checks.topic: The nine Makers of Nigeria: their parties, offices, dates and credited achievements.

questions.q: A lawyer who began practising in Lagos in 1965 took on many cases for people who could not pay, was called the people's lawyer, and from his sick bed sought to reopen the Dele Giwa parcel-bomb case. Who was he?
questions.concept: Gani Fawehinmi's credited achievements
questions.why: Gani Fawehinmi started practising in Lagos in 1965, became known as the people's lawyer for his pro bono work, campaigned for human rights for 40 years, and pressed to reopen the still unsolved 1986 Dele Giwa case. Soyinka is the playwright and Nobel laureate; Macaulay the father of Nigerian nationalism and NNDP founder; Achebe the novelist of Things Fall Apart.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs a Maker of Nigeria with the achievement credited to him or her?
options: Chinua Achebe: Nobel Prize for Literature, 1986
